Name: universal_vs_idiosyncratic_mechanisms
Title: Universal or Idiosyncratic? Using Cross-Model Representational Agreement to Separate Real Scientific Mechanisms from Training Artifacts
Short Hypothesis: Scientific concepts that reflect genuine, dataset-independent mechanisms should be encoded in the *shared* subspace across independently trained foundation models, whereas concepts that are dataset artifacts or shortcuts should live disproportionately in *model-idiosyncratic* subspaces. We hypothesize that decomposing representations into a cross-model-universal component and a model-specific component yields a 'mechanism-universality score' that (a) separates textbook mechanisms from confounds and (b) predicts out-of-distribution generalization, offering a validation route that escapes the annotation-circularity problem plaguing single-model interpretability.
Related Work: Edamadaka et al. (2025, 'Universally Converging Representations of Matter') establish that ~60 scientific models align in representation space and propose alignment as a generality benchmark, but treat convergence as a global property and do not decompose which *specific scientific concepts* live in the universal vs. idiosyncratic parts, nor connect this to mechanism validity. Orlov et al. (2026) review SAEs on biological foundation models and explicitly flag the 'circularity' problem: features are validated against annotations derived from the same training databases, so a recovered feature could be a training-set statistic rather than a real mechanism. Baek et al. (2024) study universality of graph representations in LLMs via probing and stitching but for genealogical toy tasks, not scientific mechanisms. Our proposal is novel in combining these threads: we decompose representations per-concept into universal vs. idiosyncratic subspaces across independently trained models and use cross-model agreement as a *third-party validator* of mechanism reality, directly attacking the circularity gap. This differs from my prior causal-intervention and scaling-exponent proposals, which analyze a single model in isolation.
Abstract: Interpretability studies of scientific foundation models repeatedly recover features that match known biological, chemical, and physical concepts. But as recent reviews warn, matching a feature to an annotation is circular when the annotation derives from the same databases the model was trained on: the 'concept' may be a training-set statistic, not a real mechanism. We propose a validation strategy that escapes this circularity by exploiting cross-model representational universality. The intuition: a genuine, dataset-independent scientific mechanism should be encoded consistently across models trained on different data with different architectures, so its representational axis should lie in the *shared* subspace across models; a dataset artifact or shortcut should be idiosyncratic to a model. For each scientific concept, we (1) locate its probe direction in several independently trained models, (2) use representational alignment (CKA/orthogonal alignment) to project each direction into a cross-model-universal subspace and a model-specific residual, and (3) compute a Mechanism-Universality Score = fraction of the concept's variance that is cross-model reproducible. We validate the score's meaning three ways: universal concepts should (i) survive when tested on held-out data distributions the model was not trained on, (ii) transfer via model stitching, and (iii) correlate with causal effect on outputs; idiosyncratic concepts should fail these. We apply this to open protein (ESM-2 variants, ProtBERT), molecular (multiple public chemistry transformers), and materials models across ~10 curated concepts spanning true mechanisms and known confounds, delivering an open, annotation-free audit of which 'discovered' scientific concepts are real.
Experiments: 1. Concept curation: Assemble ~10 concepts per domain paired as (true mechanism, matched confound/shortcut). Examples — proteins: hydrophobic-core burial (mechanism) vs. amino-acid frequency bias from database taxonomy over-representation (artifact); disulfide bond presence vs. organism-of-origin proxy; chemistry: aromaticity/reactivity vs. molecular-weight or dataset-source proxy; materials: composition electronegativity vs. dataset-collection-year/synthesis-route proxy. 2. Multi-model probing: For >=3 independently trained models per domain (e.g., ESM-2 8M/35M/150M, ProtBERT, ESM-1b; several public chemistry transformers; open materials encoders), fit linear probes for each concept and extract per-model probe directions and per-input concept-activation vectors. 3. Universal/idiosyncratic decomposition: Align model pairs' representation spaces via orthogonal Procrustes / CKA on a shared input set; project each concept's activation into the cross-model-shared subspace vs. residual. Define Mechanism-Universality Score = shared-subspace variance / total concept variance, averaged over model pairs. 4. Validation A (OOD survival): Hold out an input distribution disjoint from training characteristics (e.g., proteins from under-represented taxa, molecules from a different chemical space); test whether high-universality concepts retain probe accuracy on OOD while low-universality (artifact) concepts collapse. 5. Validation B (stitching transfer): Learn a linear map between two models' spaces on general inputs; test whether a concept direction learned in model A predicts the concept in model B — universal concepts should transfer, idiosyncratic ones should not. 6. Validation C (causal relevance): For concepts with an experimental counterfactual dataset (deep mutational scans for stability, reaction-yield sets), test whether universality score correlates with the concept direction's causal effect on model output (via activation steering/patching). 7. Metrics: universality score distribution for mechanism vs. confound pairs (test separation, AUROC of universality distinguishing curated mechanisms from artifacts); correlation of universality with OOD accuracy retention, stitching transfer accuracy, and causal effect size. 8. Baselines/controls: random-direction null, single-model probe-accuracy baseline (show it does NOT separate mechanism from artifact, motivating the cross-model approach), and randomly-initialized-model control. 9. Deliverable: an open, annotation-free 'mechanism reality' benchmark and per-concept universality leaderboard across public scientific models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Representational alignment across heterogeneous architectures/tokenizations may be imperfect, biasing universality estimates; mitigate with multiple alignment methods (CKA, Procrustes, SVCCA) and report agreement. 2. Two models trained on overlapping databases may share the *same* artifact, inflating universality for confounds; we address this by choosing models with maximally disjoint training corpora and reporting universality as a function of training-data overlap. 3. Linear probes may miss nonlinearly encoded mechanisms; add nonlinear-probe robustness checks. 4. Curating clean mechanism/confound pairs with independent OOD splits is nontrivial and domain-limited; some domains may only support qualitative separation. 5. Universality is a necessary but not fully sufficient indicator of mechanism validity — a shared inductive bias could produce shared artifacts; the three validation axes (OOD, stitching, causal) are designed to triangulate against this, and any failures are themselves informative. 6. Availability of >=3 truly independent open models is stronger for proteins/chemistry than materials, which may restrict that domain.
